name: Koch's Postulates
statement: Four tests to prove a specific microbe causes a specific disease.
statementAccent: a specific microbe causes a specific disease
meaning: Koch's postulates are four criteria for establishing that a particular microorganism causes a particular disease. The microbe must be found in all cases of the disease but not in the healthy; it must be isolated and grown in pure culture; the cultured microbe must cause the disease when introduced into a healthy host; and it must then be recovered from that host and shown identical to the original. Together they turn a suspected link into rigorous proof of causation.
mechanism: The four steps build a chain of causation. Finding the microbe in the diseased but not the healthy establishes association; isolating it in pure culture separates it from other agents; reproducing the disease by inoculation shows the microbe is sufficient to cause it; and re-isolating the same microbe from the newly diseased host closes the loop. Meeting all four is sufficient to establish causation, though, as later understanding shows, it is not strictly necessary, since many genuine pathogens cannot satisfy every step.

examples.text: Koch's proof that a single bacterium causes anthrax, and his identification of the tuberculosis bacterium in 1882, grew directly into the postulates.
Koch himself relaxed the first postulate on finding healthy carriers of cholera and typhoid, microbes present without disease, as in the Typhoid Mary case.
Viruses and bacteria like the leprosy and syphilis organisms cannot be grown in pure culture, so the second postulate cannot be met for them.

variants.name: Molecular Koch's postulates
variants.text: Stanley Falkow's 1988 reframing around virulence genes, addressing pathogens that cannot be grown in pure culture by tying disease to specific genes.

variants.name: The Bradford Hill criteria
variants.text: Austin Bradford Hill's broader 1965 considerations for inferring causation, used where Koch's postulates cannot apply, as in chronic and non-infectious disease.

whyItMatters: They are foundational to medical microbiology and germ theory, providing the first rigorous, reproducible method for establishing that a microbe causes a disease rather than merely accompanying it. Koch's work made him a founder of bacteriology and earned him the 1905 Nobel Prize for his tuberculosis research, and the postulates remain a reference point and a starting framework for reasoning about infectious causation.

working.text: use the four steps to turn a suspected link between microbe and disease into demonstrated causation, not mere correlation.

working.lead: Treat them as sufficient, not necessary
working.text: recognise that meeting all four proves causation, but failing to meet them does not disprove it, since many real pathogens cannot satisfy every step.
apply molecular postulates or the Bradford Hill criteria when the classical steps cannot be met, as with viruses or chronic disease.

limits: The postulates have well-known exceptions, and Koch himself abandoned the strict first postulate after finding asymptomatic carriers of cholera and typhoid. Not all pathogens can be grown in pure culture, including viruses and some bacteria, so the second postulate fails for them; deliberately infecting a healthy human host is unethical for human-only pathogens; not all exposed hosts fall ill because susceptibility varies; and some diseases are multifactorial or polymicrobial. They are best treated as a sufficient but not necessary heuristic for causation.
misreadings: It is not required that all four postulates be satisfied to prove causation; they are sufficient but not necessary, and many accepted pathogens, from viruses to the leprosy bacterium, never met the classical set. Koch did not rigidly insist the microbe be absent from all healthy hosts; he dropped that after finding asymptomatic carriers. And his 1905 Nobel Prize was for his tuberculosis investigations, not specifically for the postulates.
origin: Formulated by Robert Koch, with Friedrich Loeffler, in 1884 and refined in an 1890 address, building on Jakob Henle's earlier framework and Koch's work on anthrax and tuberculosis.
